issue_classes.hypothesis: The tracer has no notion of writing-order priors. After Hierholzer produces an Eulerian path/circuit, the start node and traversal direction are chosen by whatever the T-join/Hierholzer bookkeeping leaves first in the adjacency list, not by handwriting convention. Two systematic failures fall out: (a) vertical stems get traversed bottom-up because the path enters at the baseline foot/serif leaf the algorithm picked as the Euler start; (b) bowls (c, s, g, C, G) get traced clockwise/counter-clockwise arbitrarily because a closed loop has no canonical start and the entry edge is picked by adjacency order. Caps with arcs frequently start mid-stem or at the wrong x-extreme. There is no post-Hierholzer pass that flips each stroke to obey 'stems top-to-bottom, bowls open-side-first, left-to-right'.
issue_classes.suggested_fix: Add a writing-convention orientation pass AFTER stroke extraction and BEFORE smoothing. For each extracted stroke, score both directions against generic geometry-only priors and flip to the higher-scoring one: (1) prefer the higher-y (top) endpoint as start for predominantly-vertical strokes; (2) prefer the leftmost/topmost endpoint as start for horizontal strokes; (3) for closed/near-closed loops choose the start at the local extreme nearest the glyph's natural entry and orient so the first motion descends. Per-stroke endpoint/tangent vector test, font-agnostic, no per-letter table.

issue_classes.hypothesis: The dominant structural failure, intrinsic to using one Eulerian path for the whole glyph multigraph. Hierholzer covers every edge of a connected component in the minimum number of trails (one per component after T-join), so multi-stroke letters whose skeletons form a single connected component (H, A, E, F, K, M, R, T, Y, W) collapse into one serpentine trail. The Chinese-Postman objective minimizes retraced length, not number of natural pen-lifts, so it prefers fewer, longer, back-tracking strokes over several clean human strokes. Result reads as outline/circuit tracing and forces the back-tracking wrong_direction artefacts on arms/legs.
issue_classes.suggested_fix: Replace the 'one Euler trail per connected component' objective with a stroke-decomposition objective that splits the multigraph at junctions into natural strokes before tracing. At each degree>=3 junction, pair incident edges by tangent continuity (straight-through pairs stay in one stroke, sharp-angle pairs become separate strokes), then run Hierholzer on each resulting low-degree subgraph. Yields 2 stems + crossbar for H, two legs + bar for A, etc. Tangent-driven at junctions, generalizes across all letters with no per-letter stroke count.

issue_classes.hypothesis: Once a glyph splits into multiple strokes, emit order is whatever the component/stroke loop yields (often by node index or which Euler trail closed first), with no model of which stroke a human draws first. Symptoms: accessory strokes before the main stroke (crossbar before stem in t/f/A/T; exit-flick before body in DancingScript v/w/a; bowls before stems in p/b/d/f). No 'main structural stroke first, then accessories, generally left-to-right / top-to-bottom' ranking.
issue_classes.suggested_fix: Add a stroke-ordering pass after decomposition: sort strokes by a generic salience+position key — (1) longest/most-central structural stroke first within each spatial cluster, (2) tie-break left-to-right then top-to-bottom by start point, (3) classify short terminal strokes (length below a fraction of glyph size, attached at one end) as accessories and emit them after the structural stroke they touch. Dots/tittles stay last. Pure geometry, no per-letter ordering table.

issue_classes.hypothesis: Mirror image of under_split, driven by the skeleton/graph front-end. Two mechanisms: (a) the sharp-turn split fires on noise — at serif clusters and medial-axis spurs the skeleton produces many short degree-1/degree-3 stubs, each becoming a micro-stroke (Garamond/Arvo x fragmenting into 4-7 strokes, tiny serif stubs as separate strokes); (b) a single smooth feature (cursive s, j descender, a stem) gets cut because the medial axis wobbles past the sharp-turn threshold. Serif fonts (Garamond, Arvo) and high-curvature cursive (DancingScript) are worst because both stress the skeleton: serifs add spurs, cursive adds curvature that trips the turn detector.
issue_classes.suggested_fix: Strengthen pre-trace skeleton cleanup and make sharp-turn split hysteretic. (1) Prune skeleton spurs whose length is below a distance-transform-scaled threshold (serif flanges, medial-axis hairs) so they merge into their parent stroke. (2) Replace the single-angle split threshold with hysteresis + minimum-segment-length: split only when the turn exceeds the high threshold AND both resulting segments exceed a min length proportional to glyph size; else keep whole. Both global parameters scaled by stroke width, no per-letter logic.

issue_classes.hypothesis: The centerline leaves the ink and crosses white space. Causes: (a) at junctions where the T-join added a duplicate/connector edge, Hierholzer routes the connector through a straight skeleton chord rather than along the glyph contour, cutting across an interior valley (M, W, X inner Vs) or shooting a spur into the serif/terminal region; (b) skeleton over-extension at high-curvature terminals (Lobster j/p/x) leaves a hair of medial axis poking outside the eroded mask. This is the ghost-stray class the recent commit targeted but did not fully eliminate on cursive/serif extremes.
issue_classes.suggested_fix: Add a final on-ink validation+clip pass over every emitted centerline: sample each polyline against the source mask and (1) clip any sub-segment whose midpoint falls outside the dilated ink as a stray excursion, (2) when a T-join connector edge must bridge a gap, route it along the shortest in-mask skeleton path rather than a straight chord. Reject/trim leaf segments shorter than a width-scaled epsilon that exit the mask. Generic mask test, applies to every glyph.

issue_classes.hypothesis: An edge is traversed twice, leaving a doubled/jagged line on a stem or bar. This is the T-join / Chinese-Postman duplication surfacing as visible ink: to make the graph Eulerian, odd-degree vertices are paired and the connecting path's edges duplicated; when the cheapest pairing routes the duplicate back along a real stem (Arvo d/h stem, crossbars, Arvo Z top bar) the pen retraces it. The Y-fork arrow artefacts at stem bases (Lobster D/F) are the duplicated-edge return showing a second arrowhead.
issue_classes.suggested_fix: Make the T-join cost-aware of visibility and de-duplicate at render. (1) In odd-vertex matching, weight duplicate-edge cost by length and penalize duplicating long structural edges, so the matcher routes duplicates through short junction connectors rather than full stems. (2) After tracing, detect coincident anti-parallel sub-paths (same polyline traversed both ways within stroke-width tolerance) and collapse them to a single pass. Tangent+position coincidence test, font-agnostic.

issue_classes.hypothesis: A real feature is under-traced or absent. Distinct from over_split: here the feature gets no adequate centerline. Causes: (a) spur-pruning too aggressive, deleting short genuine features (i/j dots reduced to stubs, Garamond B stem pruned to a curl, h ascender not reaching top); (b) lower bowl of s / part of a bowl swallowed because a parallel-edge collapse or junction merge removed the branch (Lobster s lower bowl, Arvo/Lobster p bowl only partially traced); (c) animation timing makes late strokes look absent (Caveat U/X reading as J/fragment for most of the flipbook) — an ordering artefact, not missing geometry.
issue_classes.suggested_fix: Tie pruning to a feature-coverage guard (open work item 5): walk the skeleton's branches and require every branch above a width-scaled length to be covered by at least one emitted stroke; if a branch is uncovered after tracing, re-include it as its own short stroke. Make spur-pruning length threshold proportional to the local distance-transform value so genuine dots/serifs survive while medial-axis hairs are removed. The timing subset is fixed by the wrong_order ordering pass.

issue_classes.hypothesis: Catch-all for two minor effects: (1) overlapping start-marker badges when multiple strokes share a near-identical start point (Garamond m/n, clustered junction starts) — a diagnostic-rendering issue that nonetheless signals strokes spuriously sharing an origin, tying back to under_split; (2) centerline running along a stem edge rather than the true medial axis, or rounding sharp corners (Arvo l jagged, Caveat Z reads as 2) — a smoothing/skeleton-fidelity nit. Low impact.
issue_classes.suggested_fix: Two small generic fixes: anchor diagnostic start-markers to each stroke's first 2-3 points (not the shared junction pixel) so badges separate; and in smoothing, preserve corners above an angle threshold by reducing spline tension locally (corner-aware knot insertion) so Z/k angles stay crisp instead of rounding. Both global.

per_font_quality.verdict: Best performer: cursive geometry suits single-stroke tracing; failures concentrate in caps needing multi-stroke splitting (A, M, N) plus a few bottom-up stems.
Worst performer: serifs spawn spurs (over_split on x) and the single-Euler-trail collapse wrecks nearly every capital (A,B,D,E,F,H,K,L,M,T,U,V,W,Y) as outline tracing.
Lowercase mostly clean; caps and a cluster of letters suffer under_split/back-track (H,M,N,Y) and bottom-up stems (h,p,r) — solidly mid-pack.
Slab serifs are punishing: heavy over_split and stray serif spurs on x/X, double_trace on d/h stems, full single-trail collapse on A,H,K,P,Q,R caps.
Display-cursive mostly reads naturally, but flourishes generate the most stray_stroke artefacts (M,W,X,j cutting through white space) and a few bottom-up stems.
High-curvature cursive trips over_split/double_trace badly on j,s,x and reverses stroke order on connected letters (f,v,w,B,N,X); good when one stroke suffices.

default_tracer_recommendation:
Recommend a CONDITIONAL yes: make EPST the default now for lowercase and for the cursive/script fonts, but do NOT yet trust it as the sole tracer for serif capitals until two systematic defects are fixed.

Net quality: across 312 diagnostics roughly 187 letters (60%) are clean; the remaining 40% carry at least one issue but only ~78 letters (25%) carry a HIGH-severity issue, and those are heavily concentrated in serif-font capitals (EBGaramond, Arvo) and a predictable set of multi-stroke caps (A, H, K, M, N, R, T, W, Y) plus high-curvature cursive (DancingScript j/s/x). Lowercase across all six fonts is in good shape. Since EPST replaces a Hershey-template heuristic tracer whose known quality is worse, switching the default is a net improvement on the majority of glyphs and removes the per-letter Hershey LETTER_STRATEGY maintenance burden, which aligns with the project rule against per-letter hacks.

Two blocking defect classes must be fixed before EPST becomes the unconditional default, because they are systematic and visually disqualifying: (1) under_split — the single-Eulerian-trail-per-component collapse that turns H/A/E/M into mechanical outline circuits (31 occurrences, 24 high); and (2) wrong_direction — bottom-up stems and arbitrary bowl orientation (58 occurrences, 17 high). Both have clean, generalized, geometry-only fixes (tangent-driven junction splitting; a post-Hierholzer orientation pass) and neither needs per-letter tables.

Concrete rollout: (a) ship EPST as default now behind a per-glyph confidence gate — if a glyph's skeleton is a single connected component with degree>=3 junctions AND EPST would emit it as one trail spanning multiple natural strokes, fall back to the old tracer for that glyph until the splitting pass lands; (b) implement the junction-split, orientation, and stroke-ordering passes (they fix under_split, wrong_direction, and wrong_order together — ~110 of the ~170 issues); (c) then drop the gate and remove the Hershey tracer. Do not flip the unconditional default until alphabet_static.svg for EBGaramond and Arvo capitals is visually clean, since metrics alone won't catch the outline-tracing look.
